title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Ajaan Mahā Boowa talks about two methods for developing samādhi, for developing Dhamma. The first is the usual method where you practice samādhi…
content:
Two Methods for Developing Samādhi

"Ajaan Mahā Boowa talks about two methods for developing samādhi, for developing Dhamma. The first is the usual method where you practice samādhi first. When the mind can hold its attention on whatever you put it on, then you turn to investigating for the development of paññā, or wisdom. That is one method; and for many people that’s the way they must go. The other method is the method of wisdom develops samādhi, where you develop wisdom by investigating and thinking. If you continue on until you become absorbed in that investigation, samādhi will develop. It depends on each individual which way they must go. Generally speaking, we can say that if you can keep your attention firmly on the investigation, then you can probably go the way of wisdom develops samādhi. If you can't, if your mind jumps about and won't keep on what you are investigating, then you must do the samādhi to develop wisdom."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: “When you say the nature of Nibbāna is emptiness—empty of what? Empty of this world, empty of saṃsāra, and empty of the whirlwind…
content:
The Nature of Emptiness and Nibbāna

“When you say the nature of Nibbāna is emptiness—empty of what? Empty of this world, empty of saṃsāra, and empty of the whirlwind of changing phenomena. What we think of as being full is always saṃsāra. It’s always dualistic, always relative. Because of that, when those things that fill up saṃsāric existence disappear, we call it emptiness. But that emptiness is not a nothingness. It’s a reality. But because we have to think in relative, dualistic terms, emptiness is quite incomprehensible to us. Our entire existence is built up around fullness. So when we try to comprehend emptiness in relative terms, we can’t do it. Because of that, we suppose there is nothing there. But what we call a ‘thing’ is itself empty. We don’t realize that.”

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "The scientist's understanding of the world is always changing, always being revised. What was scientific fact 50 years ago is often considered primitive…
content:
Conventional vs. Ultimate Truth in Causality

"The scientist's understanding of the world is always changing, always being revised. What was scientific fact 50 years ago is often considered primitive misunderstanding today, and what passes for settled science today will likely seem quaint and outdated 50 years hence... but it shows us that science deals with conventional, relative truth, or "sammuti sacca", not the ultimate truth of "paramattha sacca". The cause-and-effect nature of reality means that nothing happens randomly or without reason. Every experience, every state of mind, every circumstance arises dependent on conditions. When those conditions change, the experience also changes. This is why the practice of "Dhamma" focuses on understanding and working with causes rather than struggling with effects. When we contemplate deeper questions like, 'Why are we here? What is the purpose of life? How should we live?', science falls silent. These questions cannot be answered by measuring brain waves or analyzing chemical reactions. They require direct investigation of the mind itself, using the methods the Buddha discovered and verified through his own experience.",

title: A. Paññāvaddho: Moderation in eating starts off with eating only that amount of food that doesn’t make you fat. That’s a simple way of putting…
content:
Principles of Moderation in Eating and the Three Types of Food

Moderation in eating starts off with eating only that amount of food that doesn’t make you fat. That’s a simple way of putting it. But moderation in eating also means that you don’t look for the choice bits of food, but you take the food as it comes. In the end, moderation in eating means that you try to eat those things that help the meditation practice. The Indians have an interesting way of putting it; they say that there are three types of food: tamas, rajas, and setva. The tamas food makes you feel heavy and thick. The rajas food is the moderate type and makes you hot, and it can increase sensuality. The setva food makes you light and buoyant and doesn’t require a lot of digestion. In general, one will probably need a combination of all three. But don’t take too much of the first two types of food because they can have a big effect on the practice.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Of course, we must steadily practice to perfect each factor of the Path; that’s necessary. But simply practicing the Noble Eightfold Path a…
content:
The Culmination of Practice in Deep Meditation

"Of course, we must steadily practice to perfect each factor of the Path; that’s necessary. But simply practicing the Noble Eightfold Path a little bit here and a little bit there won’t get us to the goal. Today we’ll do this, tomorrow we’ll do that and so on. The Noble Eightfold Path is, in effect, the path to Nibbāna. This means that it culminates in perfection at a very deep level within the mind. It’s not simply a journey from one stage to the next; its fruition requires a practice of meditation that has gone very deep, to the point where all these factors coalesce with equal strength and purpose. Only when the time and conditions are right does the path moment take place. That being said, the Noble Eightfold Path is not simple textbook Buddhism. That is something which has been misunderstood."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: As our practice deepens, we'll move beyond conceptual understanding to direct knowing. We'll see these processes clearly because we've observed them for ourselves…
content:
The Endless Stream of Mental Hunger

As our practice deepens, we'll move beyond conceptual understanding to direct knowing. We'll see these processes clearly because we've observed them for ourselves in our own experience. But keep in mind that these processes never stand still. Our thoughts and actions flow in an endless stream, like a river that never rests at any single point. Even when we get what we think we want, a new wanting quickly takes its place. Each satisfied desire gives birth to fresh desires, creating a cycle that's constantly spinning out of control. Think of how one thought leads to another: a memory triggers a worry, which sparks a plan, which then fuels an action. Each mental state feeds the next, like a flame passing from one candle to another.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "These defilements are experienced as momentary eruptions of greed, hatred, and delusion that flood moments of perception and begin to influence our behavior.…
content:
The Expressive Storm of Momentary Eruptions

"These defilements are experienced as momentary eruptions of greed, hatred, and delusion that flood moments of perception and begin to influence our behavior. We might say that this expressive level of defilements is like a storm that blows through the mind. It's only passing through, but while it's present, it can completely take over our thoughts, speech, and actions. For example, a woman is subject to criticism and feels anger begin to stir, breaking into the open. This anger disturbs her peace of mind and creates immediate displeasure. If she clings to this angry response, it may lead her to speak harshly to others or even to seek revenge, thus opening the door to unpleasant karmic consequences."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Whatever you recall, whether it is a past life was something else, you do not regress back to that recollection, instead you recall…
content:
Recalling the Past from the Perspective of the Present

"Whatever you recall, whether it is a past life was something else, you do not regress back to that recollection, instead you recall it in the present. So in that sense memory is always takes place in the present. Why do we want to recall past lives? The main reason is that we want to see the ways of cause and effect – how actions we did in that life have had results in this one. That’s valuable information. We also want to see whether our past actions have brought us happiness or suffering, pleasantness or unpleasantness. This gives us a very good perspective for the appreciation of kamma and the noble truth of dukkha."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "The one who understands these things is an aspect of the one who knows. And it is that aspect which can become free.…
content:
The Influence of Ignorance on the Knowing Essence

"The one who understands these things is an aspect of the one who knows. And it is that aspect which can become free. It has no physical characteristics and so it is not a thing of the world. It only becomes associated with the world because of the kilesas. The one who knows is infected by these defilements. That infection causes ignorance. Being pervaded by ignorance, the one who knows has no confidence in itself. Because it has no confidence in itself, it feels compelled to grab hold of things to give it confidence. So we need to have other people, other objects and sensations about us to give us confidence in our own existence."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "This is basically the way of Buddhism, the path that it goes along. The fundamental cause of why we should practice Buddhism is…
content:
Overcoming Rooted Ignorance and Wrong Actions

"This is basically the way of Buddhism, the path that it goes along. The fundamental cause of why we should practice Buddhism is the fact that we all have discontent, we are not satisfied. And so we can see that the cause of this discontent is ourselves. We have produced the causes and we have produced them because of delusion and ignorance. It is out of ignorance which is very deeply rooted and cannot be eliminated merely by learning or knowing about it. With the ordinary ignorance in the world we just learn about that thing and the ignorance of it disappears. But fundamental ignorance will not disappear so easily because it is so very deeply rooted. It is a kind of blindness where we cannot see, even when we have ignorance, because of which we are always going and doing the wrong things. And although we are doing the wrong things we think those things are right. We think that this is the way to overcome our discontent. But our fundamental understanding is wrong so it does not turn out that way. Instead, the wrong things we do we accumulate for our future. So that in the future we will experience the bad results that come from wrong actions, which equals more discontent. So we have to learn to overcome these delusions, the greed and the hate within us. If we can accomplish that then all of our problems will disappear automatically."
